title: Vec of Anything
story: You've used Vec[Int] and Vec[Str] — but Vec is itself a generic type. You can create Vec of ANY type: Vec[Bool], Vec[Float64], even Vec of your own custom types. Understanding this unlocks the full power of the collections library.
why: Vec[T] is a generic container — understanding that you can parameterize it with any type opens up Vec[YourType], Vec[Pair], and beyond.
analogy: Vec is like a shipping container. A container can hold anything: crates of apples (Vec[Str]), barrels of oil (Vec[Float64]), or boxes of machinery (Vec[YourType]). The container (Vec) doesn't care what's inside — it just provides the same push/pop/get operations. The label on the outside (Vec[Int] vs Vec[Str]) tells the dock workers what to expect.
try_it: Create a `Vec[Float64]` with five decimal numbers and write a generic `sum_vec[T]` that works on any numeric Vec. Create a `Vec[Pair[Str,Int]]` — a Vec of name-score pairs — and iterate over it. Create `Vec[Vec[Int]]` (a grid) and write a function to print it row by row.
tips: `Vec` itself is generic — `Vec[T]` means 'Vec parameterized by type T'
Write functions generic over `Vec[T]` when the logic doesn't depend on what T is
Nested generics like `Vec[Pair[Str,Int]]` are valid — the outer Vec contains Pair elements
common_mistakes: Forgetting that Vec methods like `.pop()` return `Option[T]` — the T matches whatever the Vec contains
Mixing types in one Vec — `Vec[Int]` can only hold Ints; you can't push a Str into it
Trying to create `Vec[Pair]` without specifying Pair's own type parameters — it must be `Vec[Pair[Str,Int]]`
